front: A 12:3:1 ratio indicates {{c1::dominant epistasis}}: one dominant allele masks the other locus.
why: 12:3:1 is a second-tier modified ratio; 9:3:4 is the one usually asked

front: A 9:3:4 dihybrid ratio signals {{c1::recessive epistasis}}: homozygous recessive at one locus masks the second locus.
why: Recessive epistasis 9:3:4 (Labrador) is the classic tested modified ratio

front: A bat wing and an insect wing share function but no common ancestral structure, making them {{c1::analogous}}.
why: Analogous vs homologous structures is core evidence-for-evolution material

front: A disomic gamete carries both a maternal grandmother allele and a maternal grandfather allele of one gene. Which meiotic division failed?
why: Meiosis I vs II nondisjunction reasoning; plausible passage second step

front: A dominant trait appears to skip a generation: an unaffected person has both an affected parent and an affected child. Interpret.
why: Incomplete penetrance making a dominant trait skip a generation is a classic pedigree trap

front: A fossil lineage shows long morphological stasis interrupted by rapid change. Which model does this support?
why: Punctuated equilibrium vs gradualism is a named, commonly tested contrast

front: A mule is vigorous but sterile, which is a {{c1::postzygotic}} isolating mechanism.
why: Pre- vs postzygotic isolation is core speciation content

front: A single ancestral finch lineage produces many species with distinct beak shapes on one archipelago.
why: Adaptive radiation is a named core evolution concept

front: A trait expressed only in males but encoded on an autosome is {{c1::sex-limited}}, not Y-linked.
why: Sex-limited vs Y-linked distinction; secondary pedigree nuance

front: A vestigial structure provides evidence for evolution because it:
why: Vestigial structures as evidence for evolution; basic supporting fact

front: A viral surface gene shows dN/dS greater than 1. What does that indicate biologically?
why: dN/dS ratio is a research metric beyond the AAMC outline; a passage would define it

front: An X-linked recessive affected father: what is the status of all his daughters and all his sons?
why: Affected father -> all daughters carriers, no sons is the key X-linked recessive rule

front: Contrast allopatric and sympatric speciation, and give the classic sympatric mechanism.
why: Allopatric vs sympatric speciation and polyploidy are core

front: Contrast incomplete dominance and codominance.
why: Incomplete dominance vs codominance is a high-frequency distinction

front: Define epistasis precisely, distinguishing it from dominance.
why: Precise epistasis vs dominance definition; supports the plainer epistasis card

front: Define penetrance and expressivity.
why: Penetrance vs expressivity definitions are explicitly on the AAMC outline

front: Distinguish a population bottleneck from a founder effect, then give a human example of each.
why: Bottleneck vs founder effect is core genetic drift content

front: Distinguish sex-limited from sex-influenced autosomal traits, with an example of each.
why: Sex-limited vs sex-influenced (pattern baldness) is a second-tier distinction

front: Each node on a phylogenetic tree is {{c1::an inferred common ancestor}} at which two lineages diverged.
why: Reading phylogenetic tree nodes; passage context rather than a discrete point

front: Explain 9:3:4 with pathway logic: why does knocking out an upstream enzyme hide downstream genotypes?
why: Pathway logic behind 9:3:4; supporting detail on the epistasis ratio

front: For that population, what fraction are carriers?
why: 2pq carrier calc is core, but this card dangles off the q=0.4 card ('that population')

front: Genetic drift changes allele frequencies fastest in {{c1::small}} populations because sampling error scales inversely with size.
why: Drift strongest in small populations is core

front: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium requires all EXCEPT:
why: Hardy-Weinberg assumptions are a standard discrete question

front: Homologous structures indicate:
why: Homologous structures -> divergent evolution is core

front: How can a heterozygous carrier female manifest an X-linked recessive disease?
why: Manifesting heterozygote via skewed X-inactivation; supporting detail

front: How can uniparental disomy cause an imprinting disorder without any deletion or mutation?
why: Uniparental disomy via trisomy rescue is clinical-genetics detail beyond MCAT scope

front: How do cis (coupling) and trans (repulsion) configurations change what counts as a parental gamete?
why: Cis/trans (coupling/repulsion) phase nomenclature is not tested; RF is the same either way

front: How does genomic imprinting silence an allele, and when is the imprint erased and reset?
why: Imprinting by parent-of-origin methylation; plausible passage mechanism

front: How does linkage affect inheritance?
why: Linkage and RF-proportional-to-distance is core

front: How is mitochondrial DNA inherited?
why: Maternal mitochondrial inheritance is core

front: If 16% of a population is homozygous recessive, what is $q$?
why: q from q^2 is the most basic Hardy-Weinberg calculation

front: In a conserved gene, {{c1::synonymous}} substitutions accumulate faster than nonsynonymous ones.
why: Synonymous vs nonsynonymous under purifying selection; plausible passage inference

front: In a long-term E. coli experiment, only one of twelve identical populations evolved citrate use. What does that show?
why: Named study (Lenski citrate experiment); historical contingency is not an AAMC concept

front: In a testcross of a dihybrid, parental gamete classes exceed recombinant classes. What does this reveal?
why: Excess parental classes in a testcross means linkage; standard mapping inference

front: In a three-point testcross, how do you identify the middle gene?
why: Three-point cross middle gene; gene mapping is on outline but this is prep-level depth

front: Interference equals 1 minus the {{c1::coefficient of coincidence}} (observed double crossovers over expected).
why: Interference and coefficient of coincidence are beyond MCAT scope

front: List the evidence that mitochondria descend from an engulfed bacterium.
why: Endosymbiosis evidence is tested in cell biology; belongs to another topic but earns points

front: Modified dihybrid ratios always sum to 16 because they are regroupings of the underlying {{c1::9:3:3:1}} classes.
why: Modified ratios regroup 9:3:3:1; useful reasoning heuristic for epistasis

front: Neurofibromatosis siblings share one mutant allele, yet one has skin macules and the other severe tumors. What concept is this?
why: Clinical example of variable expressivity; illustrates a tested concept

front: Only {{c1::shared derived}} characters define a clade; shared ancestral traits do not.
why: Shared derived characters define clades; cladistics appears in passages

front: Penetrance is the fraction of carriers showing {{c1::any phenotype at all}}; expressivity is the severity or form it takes.
why: Near-restatement of the plainer penetrance/expressivity definition card

front: Pleiotropy is one gene affecting {{c1::many phenotypes}}; epistasis is one gene masking another gene's phenotype.
why: Pleiotropy vs epistasis distinction is a high-frequency discrete

front: Prader-Willi syndrome reflects loss of the {{c1::paternally}} expressed 15q11 region; Angelman reflects loss of the maternal copy.
why: Prader-Willi/Angelman is the standard imprinting example

front: Random X-inactivation makes every female a {{c1::mosaic}} of clones expressing one X or the other.
why: X-inactivation, Barr body, mosaicism and dosage compensation are core

front: Reciprocal adaptation between a pathogen and its host with no net advantage gained is described by the {{c1::Red Queen}} hypothesis.
why: Red Queen hypothesis is a named idea outside the AAMC outline

front: Recombination frequency: RF = recombinants/total offspring, and 1 percent RF defines {{c1::one map unit (centimorgan)}}.
why: RF formula and 1% = 1 cM is a calculation the exam uses

front: Sexual dimorphism often results from:
why: Sexual selection explains dimorphism; basic supporting fact

front: The neutral theory of molecular evolution proposes that most variation is:
why: Neutral theory underpins the molecular clock; plausible passage context

front: Two lineages differ at 60 sites in a gene whose neutral substitution rate is $2 \times 10^{-9}$ per site per year over 1000 sites.
why: Molecular clock divergence arithmetic with 2T is not AAMC-tested

front: Under Hardy-Weinberg, an X-linked recessive allele at frequency $q$ affects males at frequency {{c1::$q$}} and females at $q^2$.
why: X-linked HW: male incidence q, female q^2 is a classic calculation

front: What are pseudoautosomal regions, and how do genes there behave in pedigrees?
why: Pseudoautosomal regions are trivia-grade for the MCAT

front: What is a test cross?
why: Test cross definition is core

front: What is epistasis?
why: Plain epistasis definition with Labrador example

front: What pedigree pattern is diagnostic of mitochondrial inheritance?
why: Mitochondrial pedigree pattern (all children of affected mother) is a standard discriminator

front: What pedigree signature suggests an imprinted gene rather than simple dominance?
why: Imprinted-gene pedigree signature is beyond what AAMC asks; imprinting example cards suffice

front: What phenotypic ratios come from monohybrid and dihybrid crosses?
why: Monohybrid 3:1 and dihybrid 9:3:3:1 ratios are foundational

front: Which molecular marker suits deep divergences, and which suits relationships within a species?
why: Choice of molecular marker for phylogenetics is methodology trivia

front: Why are vestigial structures and shared developmental patterns stronger evidence for descent than functional similarity?
why: Restates the vestigial/homology-vs-analogy cards already in the deck

front: Why are X-linked recessive traits more common in males?
why: Hemizygosity explains male excess in X-linked recessive traits; core

front: Why can recombination frequency never exceed 50 percent, no matter how far apart two genes lie?
why: RF cap at 50% = independent assortment is commonly tested

front: Why do mitochondrial diseases preferentially damage nerve and muscle?
why: Tissue tropism of mitochondrial disease with named syndromes is clinical detail

front: Why do siblings with the same mitochondrial mutation show very different severity?
why: Heteroplasmy explaining variable severity; plausible passage concept

front: Why do two-point crosses underestimate long map distances?
why: Double crossovers hiding recombinants; outline lists single/double crossovers

front: Why does a 9:7 ratio arise from two genes, and how does it relate to complementation?
why: 9:7 ratio and complementation; second-tier epistasis example

front: Why does the biological species concept fail for bacteria?
why: Biological species concept limits for bacteria; plausible discrete

front: Why must recombination mapping use a testcross to a homozygous recessive partner?
why: Why mapping uses a testcross; supporting detail on the test cross card

front: X-linked recessive pedigrees show mostly affected {{c1::males}} and never male-to-male transmission.
why: No male-to-male transmission is the key X-linked recessive pedigree signature

front: Y-linked (holandric) inheritance shows {{c1::father-to-all-sons}} transmission with only males affected.
why: Y-linked father-to-all-sons pattern; rare but a clean pedigree discriminator
